sections.title: Lesson 3.1: Characteristics of Bonds
sections.overview: Bonds are debt securities representing a loan from investor to issuer (corporations, federal government, agencies, or municipalities). This lesson covers the basic mechanics of bonds — par value, maturity structures, coupons, accrued interest, pricing, yields, features (call/put/convertible), zero-coupon bonds, bond ratings, volatility, benefits/risks of ownership, types of corporate bonds (secured vs. unsecured), and the order of liquidation in bankruptcy.
key_concepts: Par Value: Most debt securities have a par (face/principal) value of $1,000 — the amount returned at maturity. Assume $1,000 par on the exam unless told otherwise.

Maturity Types: (1) Term bond — entire principal matures at once (issuer may use sinking fund); (2) Serial bond — portions of principal mature at intervals; (3) Balloon bond — combines serial repayments before maturity with a large final principal payment. 'Series bonds' refers to savings bonds (not a maturity type).
Coupon Rate (a.k.a. nominal yield, stated yield): The fixed annual interest rate as a percentage of par. A 6% coupon = $60/year in interest; usually paid semiannually ($30 every six months).

Accrued Interest: Buyer pays seller interest earned since last coupon; new owner receives full next coupon. Corporate and municipal bonds use 30-day month / 360-day year. Treasury notes/bonds use actual days / actual year. Zero-coupon bonds do NOT accrue interest.
Pricing: Quoted in points (1 point = 1% of par = $10). A bond at 90 = $900; at 103 = $1,030. Multiply quote by 10 to get dollar price. Bonds trade at par, premium (>par), or discount (<par).
Inverse Price/Yield Relationship: Bond prices move inversely to market interest rates. Coupon rate is always fixed regardless of market price.

Yields: (1) Nominal Yield — fixed coupon; (2) Current Yield (CY) — annual coupon ÷ market price; (3) Yield to Maturity (YTM, a.k.a. basis) — annualized return if held to maturity; (4) Yield to Call (YTC) — return if called early.
Yield Hierarchy (Discount Bond): Nominal < CY < YTM < YTC. Yield Hierarchy (Premium Bond): YTC < YTM < CY < Nominal. At par, all yields are equal.
Basis Point: 1/100 of 1% (100 bps = 1%). A bond on a '5.83 basis' has YTM of 5.83%.
Call Feature: Issuer can redeem early — benefits issuer; bonds have higher coupon. Issuers call when rates fall.
Put Feature: Holder can force early redemption — benefits investor; bonds have lower coupon. Investors put when rates rise.
Convertible Feature: Allows conversion of bond into common stock of issuer. Bond at 'parity' when bond value = value of underlying shares. Convertibles pay lower coupons.

Zero-Coupon Bonds (ZR): Sold at deep discount, mature at par, pay no periodic interest. Interest taxed annually (phantom income / annual accretion of discount). More volatile than coupon bonds of same maturity.
STRIPS: Treasury-issued zero-coupon bonds — backed by full faith and credit of U.S. government.
Treasury Receipts: Zero-coupon bonds built by broker-dealers from baskets of Treasuries — NOT backed by U.S. government.
Bond Ratings: Three major NRSROs — Moody's, S&P, Fitch. Investment grade = BBB/Baa and higher. Speculative (junk/high-yield) = BB/Ba and lower. D = default. Higher rating = lower yield (risk/reward).
Volatility: Longer maturity = more volatile; lower coupon = more volatile. Duration combines both into one measure.
Benefits of Bonds: Steady income (issuer obligated to pay), greater safety/seniority over equity in liquidation.
Risks of Bonds: Default/credit risk, interest rate risk, purchasing power (inflation) risk, call risk, reinvestment risk.

Secured Corporate Debt: (1) Mortgage bonds (backed by real estate); (2) Equipment trust certificates (backed by equipment, e.g., railroad rolling stock); (3) Collateral trust bonds (backed by securities held in trust).

Unsecured Corporate Debt: (1) Debentures — backed by full faith/credit of corporation; (2) Guaranteed bonds — backed by a third party (still unsecured); (3) Income/adjustment bonds — pay interest only if BOD declares and earnings sufficient (NOT suitable for income-seeking investors); (4) Subordinated debentures — junior to other unsecured debt.

Order of Liquidation: (1) Secured debt holders; (2) Unsecured debt/general creditors (including wages, taxes); (3) Subordinated debt; (4) Preferred stockholders; (5) Common stockholders. Administrative claimants paid after secured but before other unsecured.
Settlement: Corporate and municipal bonds settle T+2; Treasuries settle T+1.
rules: Bond pricing convention: 1 point = $10 (1% of $1,000 par).
Treasury accrued interest: actual/actual day count.
Zero-coupon bonds: no accrued interest paid on purchase; phantom interest taxed annually.
formulas: Annual Coupon Payment = Coupon Rate × Par Value (e.g., 6% × $1,000 = $60)
Current Yield (CY) = Annual Coupon Payment / Market Price
Dollar Price of Bond = Quoted Price × 10 (e.g., quote of 95 = $950)
mnemonics: Discount bond yields — 'NCMC' going up: Nominal < Current < YTM < YTC (yields rise as price falls below par).
Premium bond yields — reverse order: YTC < YTM < CY < Nominal.
'Call when rates Crash; Put when rates Pop' — issuers call in falling rates; investors put in rising rates.
Secured corporate debt: MEC — Mortgage, Equipment trust, Collateral trust.
Unsecured corporate debt: DIGS — Debentures, Income, Guaranteed, Subordinated.
Liquidation order: 'Some Underground Stockholders Pay Cash' — Secured, Unsecured (general creditors), Subordinated, Preferred, Common.

sections.title: Lesson 3.2: Government-Issued Bonds
sections.overview: This lesson covers municipal securities (issued by state/local governments) and U.S. government securities (Treasuries and agencies). Municipals offer federal tax-exempt interest and divide into general obligation (GO) and revenue bonds. Treasuries (bills, notes, bonds, TIPS, STRIPS) are the safest investments available, while agency securities (GNMA, FNMA, FHLMC, FCS) provide mortgage and agricultural financing.
key_concepts: Municipal Bonds: Issued by states, local governments, U.S. territories, authorities, special districts. Interest generally federal-tax-exempt; state-tax-exempt if investor resides in issuing state. Capital gains still taxable. Settle T+2, 30/360 accrued interest.

General Obligation (GO) Bonds: Backed by full faith, credit, and taxing power of issuer. State GOs backed by income/sales/license taxes; local GOs backed by ad valorem (property) taxes. Subject to statutory debt limits; usually require voter approval.

Revenue Bonds: Self-supporting; paid from revenues of the financed project (utilities, toll roads, airports, hospitals, stadiums, dorms). NOT subject to statutory debt limits; generally no voter approval needed.
Territory Bonds: Issued by Guam, U.S. Virgin Islands, Puerto Rico — triple tax-exempt (federal, state, local) for all U.S. taxpayers.

Short-Term Municipal Notes (Anticipation Notes): TANs (tax), RANs (revenue), TRANs (tax & revenue), BANs (bond), CLNs (construction loan), GANs (grant), tax-exempt commercial paper, variable-rate demand notes.
Treasury Bills (T-Bills): Maturities of 4, 8, 13, 26, 52 weeks. Issued at a discount, mature at par. No coupon. Highly liquid; 13-week T-bill is the benchmark risk-free rate.
Treasury Notes (T-Notes): Maturities 2–10 years. Pay semiannual interest at percentage of par; mature at par.
Treasury Bonds (T-Bonds): Maturities >10 to 30 years. Pay semiannual interest; mature at par.
All Treasuries: Issued in book-entry form, settle T+1, accrued interest on actual/actual basis.
Treasury STRIPS: Treasury-issued zero-coupon bonds; backed by full faith and credit of U.S. government. Issued at discount, no stated coupon.
Treasury Receipts: Created by broker-dealers from Treasury securities; NOT backed by U.S. government, only by underlying Treasuries held in trust.

TIPS (Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities): 5, 10, or 20-year maturities. Fixed coupon rate, but principal adjusts semiannually for inflation/deflation (CPI). Interest payments fluctuate with principal. Final principal payment never less than original $1,000 par.
Agency Securities: FCA (Farm Credit Administration), GNMA (Ginnie Mae), FNMA (Fannie Mae), FHLMC (Freddie Mac), SLMA (Sallie Mae). Settle T+2.
GNMA (Ginnie Mae): Government-owned corporation; ONLY agency security backed by full faith and credit of U.S. government. Mortgage-backed; subject to prepayment risk; pays monthly.

FNMA (Fannie Mae) / FHLMC (Freddie Mac): Publicly held, government-sponsored enterprises (GSEs). Not backed by full faith and credit of U.S. government. Interest taxable at federal, state, and local levels.
Tax-Equivalent Yield: Used to compare tax-free municipal yields to taxable corporate yields. Municipal yield will always be lower than equivalent corporate yield.

Taxation of Bond Interest: Treasuries — federal taxable, state/local exempt. Municipals — federal exempt, state depends on residency. FNMA/FHLMC — taxable at all levels. GNMA — taxable at all levels. Territory bonds — exempt at all levels.
rules: GO bonds typically require voter approval and are subject to statutory debt limits.
Revenue bonds do not require voter approval and are not subject to debt limits.
Treasury securities: book-entry only, T+1 settlement, actual/actual day count.
formulas: Tax-Equivalent Yield = Tax-Free (Municipal) Yield / (100% − Investor's Tax Bracket)
Equivalent Municipal Yield = Corporate Yield × (100% − Investor's Tax Bracket)
After-Tax Yield (taxable bond) = Taxable Yield × (1 − Tax Bracket)
mnemonics: Anticipation Notes: 'TRB-CGT' — TAN, RAN, TRAN, BAN, CLN, GAN, Tax-exempt CP.
GNMA is the 'GoNuts for Mortgage Association' — the ONLY agency with full U.S. government backing.
'Bills are Bare, Notes earn iNterest, Bonds last a Bunch' — T-bills (discount, no coupon), T-notes (2–10 yrs), T-bonds (10–30 yrs).
'GO with taxes, Revenue with use' — GOs backed by taxes; revenue bonds backed by user fees.

sections.title: Lesson 3.3: Money Market and Asset-Backed Securities
sections.overview: Money market securities are short-term (one year or less), highly liquid, relatively safe debt instruments offering low returns. Asset-backed securities (ABS), including CMOs and CDOs, are created through securitization — pooling underlying assets like mortgages or loans and selling tranches with varying risk and maturity profiles to investors.
key_concepts: Money Market Securities: Fixed-income debt with one year or less to maturity. Highly liquid, very safe, low yield. Most issued at a discount, mature at face value (no separate interest payments) — exception: jumbo CDs.

Jumbo (Negotiable) CDs: Issued by banks with minimum face value of $100,000 (often $1 million+); most mature in 1 year or less. Issued at face value, pay interest. Negotiable CDs trade in secondary market — these are the money market instruments. Retail CDs are not negotiable.

Bankers' Acceptances (BAs): Short-term time draft drawn on a bank; used to finance international trade (import/export). Maturity 1–180 days, max 270 days. Issued at a discount. A.k.a. bill of exchange or letter of credit.

Commercial Paper (Prime Paper, Promissory Notes): Unsecured corporate short-term debt to finance accounts receivable or seasonal inventory. Maturity 1–270 days (most under 90 days). Issued at a discount. Issued by high-credit-quality corporations.
T-Bills: Money market Treasury security; covered in Lesson 3.2. T-notes/T-bonds with less than 1 year to maturity also count as money market instruments.

Repurchase Agreements (Repos): A financial institution sells assets with agreement to repurchase later at slightly higher price. Used to raise short-term capital. Reverse repo = dealer buys securities with agreement to resell.
Federal Funds: Excess bank reserves above FRB requirements lent overnight from one member bank to another. Very short-term; federal funds rate is the interbank lending rate.

Money Market Suitability: Suitable for liquidity, safety, short-term needs. Not suitable for long-term investors due to low yield and reinvestment risk (frequent maturity = changing reinvestment rates).

Asset-Backed Securities (ABS): Securities whose value derives from a pool of underlying assets (mortgages, auto loans, credit card receivables, leases). Created via securitization — diversifies risk and improves liquidity of underlying assets.

Collateralized Mortgage Obligations (CMOs): Asset-backed security pooling residential mortgages, divided into tranches by maturity. Pays interest to all tranches monthly, but principal payments go to one tranche at a time (shortest first). Sensitive to interest-rate-driven prepayment risk. Often backed by GNMA/FNMA/FHLMC pass-throughs.

Collateralized Debt Obligations (CDOs): Complex ABS backed by pools of nonmortgage debt — bonds, auto loans, leases, credit card debt, receivables, derivatives. Sliced into tranches by risk/return profile. Higher risk tranches pay higher yields.

Taxation Summary: Treasuries — federal yes, state/local no, interest at maturity or biannually. Municipalities — federal no, state depends, biannually. FNMA/FHLMC — taxed at all levels, biannually. GNMA — taxed at all levels, monthly. Territory bonds — exempt at all levels, biannually.
rules: Money market instruments by definition have maturity of one year or less.
Commercial paper exempt from Securities Act of 1933 registration if maturity ≤ 270 days.
Bankers' acceptances maximum maturity of 270 days.
formulas: Discount Yield (money market) = (Face Value − Purchase Price) / Face Value × (360 / Days to Maturity)
mnemonics: Money market characteristics: 'SHLS' — Short-term, Highly liquid, Low yield, Safe.
Money market instruments: 'BCD-RTF' — Bankers' acceptances, Commercial paper, CDs (negotiable), Repos, T-bills, Fed funds.
CMO = 'M for Mortgage'; CDO = 'D for Debt' (non-mortgage).
Tranche order in CMO: shortest-maturity tranche gets all principal first (FIFO principal).
Only GNMA pays MONTHLY interest (mortgage-style); all other Treasury/agency securities pay biannually.
